newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Div policy key in LucasVarity figs.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Div policy key in LucasVarity figs.

text.p: Anglo-American car components group LucasVarity Plc, which merged last year, publishes its first set of joint annual results on Tuesday, with the market keenly awaiting clarification of its dividend policy.
Since its merger, LucasVarity has seen its shares come under pressure due to confusion over whether it will maintain its dividend or cut the payout and launch a share buyback instead.
U.S. investors, from the former Varity Corporation side of the merger, had been used to a policy of share buybacks instead of dividends.
But UK investors, from the former Lucas Industries, were accustomed to dividend growth.
Another dampener for UK investors is that share buybacks are now less efficient for pension fund investors thanks to a change in domestic taxation rules.

In January, Victor Rice, chief executive of LucasVarity, said: "The board would not consider a reduction in the dividend without announcing a share repurchase programme," citing his own preference for the latter.
Analysts are split on whether the dividend will be cut to accommodate a buyback or alternatively set at around seven pence per share.
Analysts' forecasts for the dividend therefore range widely from 2.1 pence per share to seven pence.
Sanjay Jha, analyst at Williams de Broe, said: "The results meeting will be dominated by the dividend question."
He added that there was market concern that if LucasVarity had a buyback it may delay payment until 1998, leading to no effective payout this year.
Forecasts for pretax profits in the year to January 31, 1997 range from 276.1 million to 290 million, with most pitching at 280 million.
Rice said in January that forecasts of 280 million were "realistic".
There is no defined comparable figure for last year because these are the first results for the merged group.
The results will constitute five months of the merged group results and seven months of the separate entities' figures, said Lehman Brothers analyst Charles Armitage.
"Therefore, the numbers themselves are pretty meaningless as none of the synergies will have had an impact," said Armitage.
Those synergy savings will kick in in 1998, said LucasVarity earlier this year.
In December, LucasVarity announced a gloomy trading statement, so the results are expected to show far from sparkling trading, reflecting conditions across the sector.

Lehman's Armitage said current trading was likely to be "relatively poor, particularly in diesels, driven by the downturn in France. French car sales are down 20 percent in the first quarter of 1997."
"LucasVarity's special problem is its big exposure to the diesel market, particularly in France. It's been a bad, bad market this year and the group is vulnerable," said Jha.
French car sales have collapsed since special government incentives to new car buyers ended last December.
Investors will also be looking for more information on restructuring measures and whether 120 million stg of merger cost savings are still on track for delivery by the end of 1998.
